opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about Virtual Lab is that it tries to mirror how science actually gets done. Real research rarely comes from one brilliant person working alone. It comes from an interdisciplinary team: a PI who sets the direction, specialists in different areas, and people who push back and poke holes in ideas. So instead of treating a large language model as a single assistant that answers questions, we asked what it would look like to build a whole research team out of AI agents.

In Virtual Lab, there's a PI agent that leads the project. The PI agent decides what expertise it needs and creates scientist agents, for example an immunologist, a computational biologist, or a machine learning specialist. There's also a scientific critic agent whose whole job is to be skeptical and catch errors or weak reasoning. These agents hold team meetings, where they discuss the big-picture research agenda, and individual meetings, where one agent goes off and does a specific task, like writing code or analyzing results. The human researcher acts more like a high-level advisor. We give guidance at key points, but most of the discussion and work is done by the agents.

What makes it a platform for open-ended research, rather than a narrow tool, is that we don't hard-code the workflow. The agents decide which approach to take. In our main case study, we asked them to design new binders against recent SARS-CoV-2 variants. The agents decided on their own to work on nanobodies rather than full antibodies, and they assembled a computational pipeline combining tools like protein language models, AlphaFold-Multimer, and Rosetta to propose and score candidates. Then, crucially, we took their designs into the wet lab and tested them experimentally. A number of them expressed well, and a couple showed improved binding to newer variants while retaining binding to the original strain. For us, that real-world validation is what matters. It's not enough for the agents to sound smart. The science has to hold up.

I'd also say a few lessons came out of it. One is that structure helps a lot. Having explicit roles, especially the critic, and running parallel meetings and then merging the best ideas noticeably improved the quality of the output compared to just letting one model riff. Another is that the human role shifts. You spend less time on execution and more on asking the right questions and judging what's worth pursuing. I don't see this as replacing scientists. I see it as giving every researcher access to a broad, interdisciplinary team they might not otherwise have, which could really accelerate open-ended discovery across many fields beyond biology.

r001.rationale: The response describes a PI agent leading the project, choosing and creating specialist scientist agents, and coordinating their work as a team for open-ended research.

astra-6.text:
I think of Virtual Lab as a way to bring together a team of AI scientists, with a human researcher helping to set the direction. For an open-ended research problem, you usually don’t know ahead of time exactly which steps you need to take. Part of the work is figuring out the right questions, what expertise you need, and which experiments would actually be informative.

So the idea is to have an AI principal investigator working with different specialist agents. They can propose approaches, critique one another’s assumptions, and develop a research plan through meetings. The human scientist can participate at key points, providing feedback and constraints, without having to specify every individual action.

But the discussion itself is only part of science. You want that team to produce something concrete—a computational analysis, a candidate design, or an experiment—and then use the results to revise its hypotheses. That connection to empirical feedback is really important. A group of agents agreeing with one another doesn’t establish that an idea is correct.

What excites me is the possibility of making that whole loop more accessible: taking a broad scientific question, assembling the relevant expertise, and turning it into something you can test.

r001.rationale: The response describes an AI principal investigator working with specialist agents to develop plans for open-ended research, which communicates the criterion’s coordinating AI professor role.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Virtual Lab as a way to organize a team of AI scientists around a research question. A lot of scientific work is open-ended: you don’t know ahead of time exactly which experiments to run or even which expertise you’re going to need. So the goal is to go beyond having a single model answer a question and instead create a setting where different agents can propose ideas, critique each other, and develop a research plan together.

You might have an agent acting as the principal investigator and others bringing different scientific perspectives. The human researcher helps set the direction and provides feedback, while the agents work through specific questions and come back with proposals that can be tested.

The crucial thing is connecting that discussion to evidence. A convincing conversation isn’t a scientific discovery. You need computational analyses or experiments that can tell you whether an idea actually works. So I think of the platform as a way to make that cycle—from an open-ended question to a concrete, testable hypothesis—more productive, while keeping the human scientist involved in the important decisions.

r001.rationale: The response describes organizing a team of AI scientists, with one agent acting as principal investigator and others bringing different scientific perspectives. This communicates a coordinating AI lead and specialist agents working on open-ended research.
